arml-2007-power-01b.title: Self-similarity
arml-2007-power-01b.body:
If $x=\langle1,3\rangle$ then $x=1+\cfrac1{3+\cfrac1x}=1+\dfrac{x}{3x+1}$. Multiplying out, $x(3x+1)=(3x+1)+x$, so $3x^2-3x-1=0$ and $x=\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt{21}}6$. Since $x>0$: $x=\dfrac{3+\sqrt{21}}6$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3+\sqrt{21}}6$**

arml-2007-power-01c.title: Self-similarity
arml-2007-power-01c.body:
If $x=\langle3,2,1\rangle$ then $x=3+\cfrac1{2+\cfrac1{1+\frac1x}}$. Now $1+\frac1x=\frac{x+1}x$, then $2+\frac{x}{x+1}=\frac{3x+2}{x+1}$, so $x=3+\dfrac{x+1}{3x+2}$. Multiplying out: $x(3x+2)=3(3x+2)+x+1$, i.e. $3x^2-8x-7=0$, $x=\dfrac{4\pm\sqrt{37}}3$. Since $x>0$: $x=\dfrac{4+\sqrt{37}}3$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{4+\sqrt{37}}3$**

arml-2007-power-02a.title: Locate $\langle kangle$
arml-2007-power-02a.body:
A purely periodic number with period $1$ has all $a_i$ equal to some positive integer $k$, i.e. it is $\langle k\rangle$ for $k=1,2,3,\dots$ (distinct $k$ give distinct numbers by uniqueness of the expansion).

If $x=\langle k\rangle$ then $x=k+\frac1x$, so $x^2-kx-1=0$ and (as $x>0$) $x=\dfrac{k+\sqrt{k^2+4}}2$.

Since $k<\sqrt{k^2+4}<\sqrt{k^2+4k+4}=k+2$, we get $\dfrac{k+k}2<x<\dfrac{k+(k+2)}2$, i.e. $k<\langle k\rangle<k+1$.

Hence $\langle k\rangle<K$ exactly when $k\le K-1$: indeed for $k\le K-1$, $\langle k\rangle<k+1\le K$, and for $k\ge K$, $\langle k\rangle>k\ge K$. So the numbers are $\langle1\rangle,\dots,\langle K-1\rangle$, which is $K-1$ numbers. ∎

arml-2007-power-02b.title: Use $\langle 1,k\rangle$
arml-2007-power-02b.body:
For each integer $k\ge2$ consider $x_k=\langle1,k\rangle=1+\cfrac1{k+\cfrac1{x_k}}$. It is purely periodic with period exactly $2$ (the two entries $1\ne k$ differ, so period $1$ is impossible).

Since $k+\frac1{x_k}>1$, we have $0<\cfrac1{k+\frac1{x_k}}<1$ and hence $x_k<2<10$.

By uniqueness of continued fraction expansions, different $k$ give different numbers. So there are infinitely many such numbers. ∎

arml-2007-power-03a.title: Size argument
arml-2007-power-03a.body:
Since $2=\sqrt4<\sqrt6<\sqrt9=3$, we have $0<3-\sqrt6<1$.

A purely periodic number $\langle a_1,\dots\rangle$ equals $a_1+(\text{a positive number})$ with $a_1\ge1$, so it is greater than $1$. Hence $3-\sqrt6$ is not purely periodic. ∎

arml-2007-power-03b.title: Run the Euclidean-style algorithm
arml-2007-power-03b.body:
Since $4<2+\sqrt6<5$, a purely periodic representation must start with $a_1=4$. Then
$$2+\sqrt6=4+(\sqrt6-2)=4+\cfrac1{\frac1{\sqrt6-2}},\qquad \frac1{\sqrt6-2}=\frac{\sqrt6+2}{2}.$$
Since $2<\frac{\sqrt6+2}2<3$, $a_2=2$ and $\dfrac{\sqrt6+2}2=2+\dfrac{\sqrt6-2}{2}=2+\cfrac1{\frac{2}{\sqrt6-2}}$ with $\dfrac2{\sqrt6-2}=\sqrt6+2$, which is the number we started with.

So $2+\sqrt6=4+\cfrac1{2+\cfrac1{2+\sqrt6}}$ and therefore $2+\sqrt6=\langle4,2\rangle$ (period $2$). ∎

arml-2007-power-04.title: Relate $x$ and $y$
arml-2007-power-04.body:
From the continued fraction, $x=a+\dfrac1y$ (the tail after $a$ is exactly $y=\langle b,a\rangle$) and symmetrically $y=b+\dfrac1x$.

Then $xy=ay+1$ and $xy=bx+1$, so $ay=bx$ and $\dfrac xy=\dfrac ab$.

**Answer: $\dfrac ab$**

arml-2007-power-05a.title: Size argument
arml-2007-power-05a.body: A purely periodic number is $a_1+(\text{positive})>1$. If $x$ is purely periodic then $x>1$, so $0<\frac1x<1$, and $\frac1x$ cannot be purely periodic. ∎

arml-2007-power-05b.title: Euclidean algorithm terminates
arml-2007-power-05b.body:
Let $x=\frac mn>0$ be rational with $m,n$ positive integers. Write $\frac mn=a_1+\frac{r}{n}$ with $a_1=\lfloor\frac mn\rfloor$ and $0\le r<n$ (so $r=m-a_1n$). If $r=0$ the expansion ends. Otherwise $\frac mn=a_1+\cfrac1{n/r}$, and we repeat with $\frac nr$, whose denominator $r$ is strictly smaller than $n$. The denominators form a strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, so the process stops: the continued fraction of a rational number is finite.

A purely periodic number has an infinite expansion, and by uniqueness of the expansion it cannot equal a finite one. Hence it is not rational. ∎

arml-2007-power-06.title: Möbius maps
arml-2007-power-06.body:
Let $x=\langle a_1,\dots,a_k\rangle$. Then $x=a_1+\cfrac1{a_2+\cfrac1{\ddots+\cfrac1{a_k+\frac1x}}}$ (the tail after $a_k$ is $x$ again).

The map $t\mapsto a+\frac1t=\frac{at+1}{t}$ corresponds to the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (composition of such maps corresponds to multiplying the matrices). Hence $x=\dfrac{Qx+R}{Sx+T}$ where
$$\begin{pmatrix}Q&R\\S&T\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a_1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a_2&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\cdots\begin{pmatrix}a_k&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
All entries are non-negative integers; by induction $Q,R,S\ge1$ (multiplying a matrix with non-negative entries on the left by $\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ gives the new first row $(aQ+S,\ aR+T)$ and second row $(Q,R)$, and the last factor already has $Q=a_k\ge1$, $R=S=1$).

Clearing the denominator, $Sx^2+Tx=Qx+R$, i.e. $Sx^2+(T-Q)x-R=0$, a quadratic with integer coefficients. ∎

arml-2007-power-07.title: Product of roots
arml-2007-power-07.body:
By problem 6 (and its proof), $x$ is a root of $Sx^2+(T-Q)x-R=0$ with integers $S,R\ge1$. Since $x$ is purely periodic it is irrational (problem 5(b)), so $E$ is not a perfect square, and the conjugate $\bar x=D-\sqrt E$ is also a root of this integer quadratic (the quadratic is, up to a constant, the unique one with root $x$ of the form $z^2-2Dz+(D^2-E)$).

The product of the roots is $x\bar x=\dfrac{-R}{S}<0$. Since $x>0$, we get $\bar x<0$. ∎

arml-2007-power-08.title: Transposed matrices
arml-2007-power-08.body:
Let $M(a)=\begin{pmatrix}a&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, a symmetric matrix. As in problem 6, $x=\dfrac{Qx+R}{Sx+T}$ with
$$\begin{pmatrix}Q&R\\S&T\end{pmatrix}=M(a_1)M(a_2)\cdots M(a_k).$$
For $y$ the product is in the opposite order: $M(a_k)\cdots M(a_1)=\big(M(a_1)\cdots M(a_k)\big)^{\!\top}$ (since each $M(a_i)$ is symmetric and the transpose reverses products) $=\begin{pmatrix}Q&S\\R&T\end{pmatrix}$. So $y=\dfrac{Qy+S}{Ry+T}$, i.e.
$$Ry^2+(T-Q)y-S=0.\qquad(\ast)$$

Now $x$ is irrational (problem 5(b)), so any integer quadratic with root $x$ is a constant multiple of $Sx^2+(T-Q)x-R$: $(A,B,C)=\lambda(S,\,T-Q,\,-R)$ for some $\lambda\ne0$. Then
$$Cy^2-By+A=\lambda\big(-Ry^2-(T-Q)y+S\big)=-\lambda\big(Ry^2+(T-Q)y-S\big)=0$$
by $(\ast)$. ∎

arml-2007-power-09.title: Reverse number
arml-2007-power-09.body:
Let $y=\langle a_k,\dots,a_1\rangle$ be the reversed purely periodic number. By the proof of 8, $y$ satisfies $Ry^2+(T-Q)y-S=0$.

If $x$ and $\bar x$ are the roots of $Sz^2+(T-Q)z-R=0$, substitute $z=-\frac1w$: $\frac S{w^2}-\frac{T-Q}{w}-R=0$, i.e. $Rw^2+(T-Q)w-S=0$. So the roots of the equation for $y$ are exactly $-\frac1x$ and $-\frac1{\bar x}$.

Now $-\frac1x<0$ (as $x>0$), whereas $y>1$ (purely periodic). Hence $y=-\dfrac1{\bar x}$. From $y>1$ and $\bar x<0$ (problem 7): $\frac1{-\bar x}>1$ so $0<-\bar x<1$, i.e. $\bar x>-1$. ∎

arml-2007-power-10a.title: Conjugate bound
arml-2007-power-10a.body:
If $f(n)+\sqrt n$ is purely periodic then (problems 7 and 9) its conjugate satisfies $-1<f(n)-\sqrt n<0$, i.e. $\sqrt n-1<f(n)<\sqrt n$.

Since $\sqrt n$ is irrational, the open interval $(\sqrt n-1,\sqrt n)$ contains exactly one integer, namely $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. So at most one integer $f(n)$ is possible. ∎

arml-2007-power-10b.title: Identify the integer
arml-2007-power-10b.body:
From part (a), $\sqrt n-1<f(n)<\sqrt n$, and the only integer in this interval is $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. So $f(n)=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$, the greatest integer not exceeding $\sqrt n$.

**Answer: $f(n)=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$**

arml-2007-power-10c.title: Use the conjugate bound
arml-2007-power-10c.body: If $z<0$ is an integer then $z\le-1$, so the conjugate $z-\sqrt n<-1$. By problems 7 and 9 a purely periodic number $D+\sqrt E$ has conjugate in $(-1,0)$. Hence $z+\sqrt n$ is not purely periodic. (Equivalently, the only possible integer part is $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor>0$ by 10(b).) ∎

arml-2007-power-10d.title: Use $f(n)=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$
arml-2007-power-10d.body:
By part (b), $1+\sqrt n$ can only be purely periodic if $1=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$, i.e. $n\in\{1,2,3\}$; $n=1$ is a perfect square, so $n=2$ or $n=3$.

- $n=2$: $x=1+\sqrt2$ satisfies $x^2-2x-1=0$, i.e. $x=2+\frac1x$, so $1+\sqrt2=\langle2\rangle$ (this was problem 1(a)).
- $n=3$: $x=1+\sqrt3$ satisfies $x^2-2x-2=0$. For $\langle2,1\rangle$ we have $x=2+\cfrac1{1+\frac1x}=2+\frac x{x+1}$, i.e. $x^2+x=2x+2+x$, $x^2-2x-2=0$ with positive root $1+\sqrt3$. So $1+\sqrt3=\langle2,1\rangle$.

**Answer: $n=2$ gives $\langle2\rangle$; $n=3$ gives $\langle2,1\rangle$.**
